utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we proceed with the cross-examination of Mr. Kirudja, there are a few procedural matters I'd like to deal with very quickly. The first matter I'd like to raise is the status of submitted intercepts. On the 12th of November of this year, the Prosecution has indicated through an informal communication that Exhibits P618, P628, P631, P641, P645, P650, P665, P673, P677, P678, P683, P684, P685, and P715, that they should remain under seal as most of them contain signatures of the operatives who have typed the transcript. As for P618, which is the authentification spreadsheet, that is hereby put under seal to protect the identity of Witness JF-002. As far as the other 13 exhibits are concerned, I'd like to hear whether there's any objection by the Defence teams against having them under seal. I just gave the main reason why. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I've carefully checked that those numbers in addition to P618 which I just mentioned, which are as always accurately written down by our transcriber and on the record, that they are all from now on under seal. Madam Registrar, is that sufficient guidance for you?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we move to the next item. The Chamber invited the parties to -- we set a dead-line, as a matter of fact, for submissions in relation to the admissibility of the testimony of Witness JF-052. The Stanisic Defence failed to meet that dead-line but have now requested to have an opportunity respond to the Prosecution's submission and it's already indicated by Mr. Jordash that of course, if the Prosecution would then feel the need to respond to that, that he would not oppose such a further, I should say, reply, would not oppose against such a reply. Mr. Groome, what is the position of the Prosecution in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution does not object to the Chamber giving Mr. Jordash the additional time he requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I don't think, as a matter of fact, that you indicated how much time you needed, mainly that you wanted to respond. How much time do you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would be able to have seven days please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, of course, after the dead-line of the 10th of November is quite a bit, if we then also ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just thought, Your Honour, given what is happening perhaps with the next witness, then we could do it within three days, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we say this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to respond to the Prosecution's submission and that should be received by this week Friday close of business. I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could Mr. Kirudja be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you are called again to be further

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: it is such a long time ago that you've given a solemn declaration, usually if it's within one or two days we won't repeat that, but since it was the 26th of August, 2009, I'd like to invite you to again make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Would you please stand and make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. Please be seated. Mr. Kirudja, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Mr. Petrovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kirudja. I have a few questions for you. First of all, since we know that you arrived in the former Yugoslavia in April 1992, so first of all, can you tell us when UNPROFOR forces became deployed in the territory of the current Republic of Croatia, which at that time was the territory of the Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. We are talking about events of 1992. As I recall, I arrived in that part of the world around April of 1992. There already were beginnings of deployment for UNPROFOR, what then was known as UNPROFOR, in stages and in different parts. So there isn't an exact date when you could say -- at least I recall all the forces had been deployed since they began to arrive from the various nations where they came from in stages and in different parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, do you know when the deployment of UNPROFOR forces first started? Could you at least give us a month, if you know. If you don't, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I couldn't give you the exact month where they started, but I do know by the time I got there, certain forces, for example, some forces were already in Sarajevo, some forces were already in Banja Luka, Banja Luka for logistics, some forces were in the Krajina where I was destined to go, at least two battalions were already on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At what point in time did UNPROFOR reach its full operational strength? When did all UNPROFOR's forces arrive and when were all finally deployed in the territory they were supposed to cover?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I could tell you when the full strength were available in the sector of responsibility that was mine, and that was Sector North. For all other deployment, you would have to cross-examine or examine the force commander for overall answer to your question. As for those forces that were deployed in Sector North where I had responsibility, I believe the last battalion to arrive of the three battalions that was there was the Nigerian Battalion, that probably was to its full strength by July or August of 1992. I can't be very exact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, is there any dispute about these well documented matters on which I would expect it would be relatively easy to agree? Or is there any specific issue which you would like to raise, then perhaps you do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thought that I would be able to raise a very specific issue. However, in view of the witness's answer, I'm not able do that and with your leave, I'm going to move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you arrived in the territory of Sector North, is it true that all decisions regarding the military units of the Serbian side were made by the JNA staff in Bihac under the command of General Nikovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have testified to my understanding that all units that were deployed in Sector North were under the command of the general you have mentioned, Nikovic, and by units, I mean the Serbian units that were there at the time we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, pursuant to advance plan which is the basis of the UNPROFOR forces deployment, there would have been demilitarisation in the area of protected UNPROFOR zones. How do you understand demilitarisation? What was supposed to happen according to that plan in that area and how did things actually look in practice?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean pursuant to Cyrus Vance Plan, not the advance plan? I understand your question has to do with the deployment according to the Vance Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan was very specific that there would be, among other terms of that plan, a total disarmament of all military units from what was called United Nations protected areas, all of them had to be demilitarised; that is, according to the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, sir, tell us, please, did there come a time when the JNA had withdrew from that area? What happened to the weapons they had and the officers that were members of those JNA units that had been deployed in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goal -- first, the goal was that the weapons had to be turned over to designated storage areas wherein there would have been under the dual control of UNPROFOR forces called double-key control of the UNPROFOR forces and those commanders of the units that turned over those forces. That was the goal. The practice was it took a long time to get in semblance or any meaning to disarmament or turning over of those forces to UNPROFOR -- those weapons to UNPROFOR. I don't recall when, but it was much later towards the end of 1992 when we had semblance of turning over of the weapons, demilitarisation of the units so that control would be under UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were the weapons indeed placed under UNPROFOR control or was it soon retaken over and used by the units of the Army of Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, we had a brief period when they were turned over to a unit of UNPROFOR. It didn't last very long, again events have passed, it's a long time, but if my memory serves me correct, something did happen towards November and December of that year when they were taken over again and refighting did break up starting from Slenica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about November or December 1992, right, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a meeting in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the record, I think you said that you confirmed what Mr. Petrovic put to you that it was November, December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, to the best of my recollection it's around that time when something happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just you were speaking very softly and your words might have been missed. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please. Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, could you switch on your --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, in your statement which you provided in 1999, you describe in some detail the period that we are talking about. I'm going to ask you about a meeting which took place immediately after your arrival in the area. The meeting took place on the 21st of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 2D325, page 6. This might help to jog his memory, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is a meeting that you attended with Colonel Tarbuk. Do you remember that meeting, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It should be somewhere in the middle of the long first paragraph. Colonel Tarbuk addressed you, he approached you as the TO commander, and you state that at the time he was still a JNA colonel; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember this meeting that General Nambiar was the force commander also was present and I recognise, yes, that there was a Colonel Tarbuk, among others, attending that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, Colonel Tarbuk told you that he was the TO commander, although he was actually a JNA colonel. Mr. Kirudja, what can you conclude about a link that existed at the time between the TO and the JNA? Is there anything that you can conclude about that link from the fact that Colonel Tarbuk introduced himself to you as a TO commander?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose by TO you mean what I'm calling in that report as Territorial Defence force; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of this date, it's nothing special, I could attribute to Colonel Tarbuk introducing himself as JNA because at that particular point in time we had not taken over control of any part of the territory we were supposed to deploy UNPROFOR. As testimony elsewhere about that period would also indicate the overall commander was General Nikovic. He had made clear they were all JNA officers up to that particular point in time, so Colonel Tarbuk saying he was JNA commander was, to my understanding of it at that point, was of no special importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand your answer a properly, the way you understood the situation at the time was that all troops under arms in the territory were under the command of General Nikovic who was based in Bihac; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kirudja, on page 7 of your statement that we have before us at the moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in on the central paragraph on page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Here you are talking about your meeting with General Nikovic, and during that meeting he spoke about the JNA withdrawal and he said that all officers who hail from the territory of Republika Srpska Krajina would remain in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and that all JNA weapons and equipment would also remain in the same territory, that they would not be evacuated anywhere. My question to you, sir, is this: What General Nikovic said, was it actually implemented in practice, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were getting ready at that point to implement the Vance Plan. General Nikovic was well-versed with the terms of that Vance Plan and he was setting in motion the process and mechanism by which control would go to UNPROFOR. And in that context, he mentioned what is in that paragraph about everybody else who didn't come or was not indigenous, if I might use that word, to the sector, and would have to relinquish control and return elsewhere since JNA was not being disbanded all over the former Yugoslavia, it was just in the territories that control had to be turned over to UNPROFOR. In that context, yes, he said those commanders who were not from there would have to relinquish command. Yes, eventually those who relinquished command were basically those who commanded Banja Corps in Banja side. Those in Kordun, particularly Colonel Bulat, remained in control almost throughout the term that I was in Sector North because he came from that territory, so there was very little change in Kordun region, but there was a good number of changes in Banja where Colonel Tarbuk came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then General Nikovic said that the weapons and equipment would be left behind, that's what he said, and that's how things actually transpired; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all weapons. You could go into that details there, only those weapons that they needed -- or let me rephrase that. There were some weapons he excluded as not to be left in the area. Those were heavy weapons that they withdrew. I couldn't be now very clear which they were, but, yes, you are right, a good amount of other weapons were left into the hands of the commanders and those were the weapons your earlier question related to, those which were to be turned over for -- to UNPROFOR and the double-key control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you also state that Nikovic said that the -- when the JNA withdrew, they would leave behind the rockets, anti-aircraft weapons, armoured vehicles, tanks. In the course of your tour of duty, which lasted over two years, did you see any of the weapons that Nikovic mentioned? Were those weapons first stored in depots and a lock and later on in the hands of the troops of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had occasion to see lots of weapons as there were flare-ups of fightings during those two years. Not only to see them, I had seen them being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. And let's go back to a period before the JNA withdrawal, let's look at page 9 in your statement. Is it true that in the territory that you covered, which was the territory of Sector North, as many as 12 brigades of the JNA had been deployed before April 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before April 1992 you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can't vouch to how many were deployed before that, but on arrival in 1992 as that report shows, I was being informed those -- at least those units listed there were all deployed. Whether they were the only ones, whether there were more than that, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In other words, in April 1992 in Banja and Kordun there were at least 12 JNA brigades, is that correct, if I understood your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, there is a list on that report. I'm trying to count how many there are to confirm your question. How many, did you count those ones, listed there?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have done that for you, Mr. Kirudja. There are 12 listed there.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then in that sense, I would say at least those which I identified there were there, or I was told they are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, do you know how many troops or what the manpower is is in terms of numbers, so how many thousands of men would these 12 brigades actually comprise?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Had I known that, I would have actually included their numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja. But certainly it's probably several thousands of troops, correct, we can agree on that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the nomenclature, and, Your Honour, I'm not a military person, so my understanding of things military is, you would say, not that of a military person. So as I understand a brigade is bigger than a battalion, a battalion is bigger than a company, and so on. From the point of view of a battalion, a battalion is around 1.000, so there would be about 12.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, in all seriousness, did you consider brigades of less than 80 persons, which brings them well above the thousand, brigades less than 160 persons? I mean, Mr. Kirudja is not an expert. Twelve brigades is -- what is the specific relevance of knowing whether it's three, five? I mean, 12 brigades is 12 brigades, a considerable number of soldiers, I would say. And then there may even be documentation, but to bother Mr. Kirudja with that, might not be the best way to get the knowledge we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree that Mr. Kirudja can shed no more light on this, but I do trust that you understand that this is significant for the position of the Defence, but I will move on and I will not dwell on this topic any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, would you please now take a look at page 10 of your statement, your 1999 statement. You relayed there a meeting with Mr. Nikovic, that's in the last paragraph on page 10. General Nikovic explains that he has dismissed the idea to capture Zagreb and Karlovac but that he has decided to chase away the Croatian army across the Kupa and Mreznica and to establish a natural border between Croatia and Serbian Krajina. My question for you is this: First of all, do you recall having this conversation with General Nikovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the UNPA area border did in fact run along the Kupa and Mreznica rivers as mentioned by General Nikovic there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was very early. He was explaining the presence of the -- or rather, he was explaining the confrontation line where it physically was, and as the paragraph says, the confrontation line had the two forces facing each other around that area divided by the rivers Mreznica and Kupa river, and it went, as the paragraph implies at length to explain why they stopped where they stopped, and that, I believe, the paragraph makes clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, for those who are following the testimony in B/C/S, do we have the right page in front of us? If you are talking about the 4th of April meeting, then I think we need the next page in B/C/S, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was referring to English version pages, I can take a look, I don't really have the B/C/S version before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if that is important, I believe that the Serbian translation is, in fact, a page before, or rather, the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now the right page is on our screens for those following the testimony in B/C/S. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood this correctly, General Nikovic told you that instead of pushing his forces all the way to Zagreb, he stopped them at Kupa and Mreznica rivers, have I understood your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 11 in English and that will probably be page 12 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, if there's any link to the testimony given by Mr. Kirudja, then, of course, because that's in evidence, these statements are not in evidence, are not tendered, so therefore it might be easier for the Chamber to follow the evidence if you would refer to where we find relevant portions in the testimony which is in evidence, which is P47. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am afraid that P47 does not contain all these details that we felt were important, I'm not tendering this statement into evidence. I'm just using it in order to assist Mr. Kirudja to refresh his memory, and to answer the questions independently irrespective of the statement. That was the only reason I was referring him to this statement bearing in mind that this is a rather lengthy statement and Mr. Kirudja has already testified in a number of cases, I believe it's simpler this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber will miss some context but please proceed if no direct link can be made to P47. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you had another meeting with General Nikovic, one of many, and I'm referring to the meeting where the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina is also being discussed, where General Nikovic explains that Serbian forces in Bosnia will establish their own army, that the equipment and the arms in Bosnia will be in the hands of the Serbs, according to the new system -- according to a local-based system. And once all that is accomplished, 80 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be under Serbian control. Do you remember whether General Nikovic said these things to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, please directly me to the exact paragraph on the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, that's in the third paragraph on page 11. The bottom part of the second -- the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on that for Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, as far as you know, did things actually transpire the way General Nikovic described in this meeting that you had in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, counsel, when you say "things," specifically you mean what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will be specific. First of all, is it correct that Serb forces established their own military in Bosnia and that they took over JNA weapons, weapons that had been used by the JNA in that territory, in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is that fact correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my testimony where I'm saying very specific things as its evident are what I observed within Sector North where I was. The question relates to what happened outside of Sector North which was under responsibilities of others. While I understand the question the counsel is asking, I can only say in general it was my understanding that the Serbs in various forms and groups did exercise control on various parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina using weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a general understanding rather than a fact which you know from personal observance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The facts would only relate the incidences. For example, when I am travelling through those territories and I'm stopped by the unit, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you have no direct knowledge about Bosnia. You can just confirm that these were the words of General Nikovic and that is sufficient for my purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this is a good time for our break or would you like me to move on to a new topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think we should take a break. But before doing so, Mr. Groome, most of the evidence elicited now from Mr. Kirudja, are these contention issues? Is there any dispute about what happened with weapons, what was the gist of the Vance Plan, demilitarisation? Is this -- has this ever been explored whether there is any dispute about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, most of this is a matter of public record and if Mr. Petrovic presents me with the facts that he would seek agreement on, I think as long as I'm able to verify in the public record, I will agree to those facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, you may understand why I asked this question to Mr. Groome. My next question to you is how much time would you still need for further cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, another 30 minutes at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which brings you well above the one hour estimate, isn't it, which was in quite some respects dealing with matters which most likely are not in dispute, are not contested, but this has been insufficiently explored. How much time would you really need to elicit evidence which is not related to matters you could have easily agreed upon most likely?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I understood you correctly, I have used up 40 minutes and I'm requesting an additional 30 minutes, which would be an hour and 10 minutes, and, well, I will cut my interrogation short by 10 minutes and then I will be within the time-frame that I've announced of one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. During the break, I tried to have a word with Mr. Groome and I asked him -- or, rather, I tried to raise an issue about the Defence thesis which is that the accused had nothing to do with the arming of the Serbian forces in Croatia and Bosnia. Mr. Groome, however, is -- was not in a position to state his view about that. He will be after he has looked at other evidence added -- at his disposal. That was the reason why I followed a certain line of questioning and we will continue to follow the same line of questioning until we get sufficient confirmation for our thesis. With your leave, I would like to continue with my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, in your statement you also mention an agreement which was signed by Radovan Karadzic and Fikret Abdic. You mentioned that agreement on page 43 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please display that page for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you whether such an agreement was indeed reached by Karadzic and Abdic with the mediation of President Milosevic? It would be the penultimate paragraph on page 43.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I take note of that paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that such an agreement was indeed reached? I would also kindly ask you to look at 2D99, and after you have done that, could you please tell us whether that is the text of the agreement that was signed by Karadzic and Abdic with Milosevic's mediation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please note what that paragraph is saying: Fikret Abdic was saying to me that there was that agreement in the paragraph. He is saying we signed it. I had -- if you could look at that paragraph again. I personally -- at least to my recollection, at the point when he was talking to me about that agreement, I didn't have that agreement or he didn't show the agreement to me. Later on, it was clear because -- it was clear that the agreement did indeed exist since Fikret kept bringing it up, and at some point, I don't recollect where, even Milosevic did confirm that they had the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, according to what you know about the agreement, could you please look at the document on the right-hand side of the screen. First look at the first page, then we will call up all the other pages, and after you have done that, could you please tell us whether those pages correspond to what Abdic told you about that agreement that he had signed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot be a witness about the content of this agreement. It never came up. Therefore, I couldn't say it is this particular agreement Fikret Abdic was talking about or some version of it at a certain point. I simply can't testify to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked, but perhaps you can't answer the question as well, whether what he told you whether, but then, of course, you would have to read the whole of the agreement first, whether that reflects what is found in the agreement. Mr. Petrovic, is that what you intend the witness to do, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if my learned friend Mr. Groome does not dispute the fact that this is indeed the agreement that was signed by the two people I mentioned, I would like to table it if nothing else, and maybe that will speed the whole process along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to bar table the agreement? Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, after the start of court today, I received over 250 documents. If I'm given over night, I can try to verify that it is a copy, but it's just -- I'm just after getting the documents printed and still working my way through this vast volume of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, there are different issues. First of all, the witness, if he has any specific recollection about the content of the agreement as he was told by Mr. Abdic, then you can ask him about it. I don't know whether his recollection allows him to say something about it. If so, then you could ask yourself whether this agreement is the agreement. We can compare his testimony with what we read. You also could ask the witness to do that but then you would have to give him an opportunity to read that in full detail, which, of course, doesn't make much sense if he has no recollection of the details of what Mr. Abdic told him. If you want to bar table the document, then that's a different matter. If you want this document to be in evidence, then you could ask Mr. Groome whether it's of any -- whether he would object to this document being in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to correct, I misspoke, it's 250 page, not 250 individual documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That makes matters not simple, but easier. Mr. Petrovic, make up your mind on how you want to use your time and what you actually intend to establish and what evidence you want to elicit from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I only ask you to make up your mind, tell us what you want, or do what you intend to do and then we can proceed. If you want to bar table it, we could immediately ask Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what seems to be the problem? The problem lies in the fact that I want to achieve as much as and fast as I can with this witness. I'm going to talk to Mr. Groome, but before that, let me move on. Just one more question about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, do you know that Mr. Fikret Abdic signed a similar agreement with Mate Boban, the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my recollection. Mate Boban? Not to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Now, let's move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you testified that immediately upon your arrival in Sector North, you met somebody whose name was Slobodan Lazarevic, and further on you testified that during your tour of duty there and during the contacts with that person, you arrived at the conclusion that you should not take any information received from him for granted, but rather that whatever you heard from him should be double-checked against other sources. What made you reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. The counsel's summary is correct about that witness. I have testified several times that there were a number of events that led me to make that conclusion. It wasn't one or two events, there were a number of events. They came in sequence because I had no reason at the beginning to make that conclusion, so the conclusion is deferring to came much later. And he is correct, I had then concluded, yes, I'll keep my lines open to him but whatever he said, I needed collaborated and checked and cross-checked for the reasons of earlier events that I have testified to and he knows from the report, those are the events connected to Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you also testified that Lazarevic had hindered the work of the United Nations staff and that he also controlled the persons who were worked for the United Nations. How did Lazarevic control your work in Sector North? How did he hinder your work there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might change your wording. He attempted to control, not that he controlled. He attempted on various occasions to influence who we hired. I will mention at least one quick incidence that the counsel might know from the testimony. The case of the interpreter Indira, you might have it over there, where he did force her evacuation from Topusko to Bihac. There were other instances but they were attempt, they were not that I concluded he can or did control, but I said he attempted time and time again to influence the -- what we did from his perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you testified that Lazarevic was also responsible for Indira's arrest. Why did Lazarevic have the lady arrested or why did he help the authorities arrest her, and how did he do that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall very broadly, this is an interpreter, among others, located on our headquarters, which at that time was in Topusko. I arrived at the end of the day from some other engagement to find that she has been arrested by the chief of police in Vrgin Most. Upon inquiries from the chief, there were a number of accusations that were made against her. In the process of trying to find out from the Vrgin Most chief, I initiated a series of events that led to a meeting with one -- now, some of these names escape me, but that was the person who was the deputy to Martic, chief of police. At that meeting that when I learned that the holding had been orchestrated by Lazarevic. I'm summarising a lot of testimony that is on record in detail. And that was when we, for her security, I mean Indira's security, we let her operate out of Bihac where they could not exercise the same kind of influence that led to her arrest. She was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn about the reasons why Lazarevic had orchestrated that arrest?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I established that he and the chief of the police in Vrgin Most were acting to cause her arrest, the reasons didn't matter. I objected to the arrest and wanted them to stop interfering and that's what they promised. After a meeting where Lazarevic was present, Cedo Bulat was present, that Deputy Tomatic [phoen], who, for the life of me, the name doesn't come up to my memory as quickly, and if I remember it, I will, he was in there. I obtained their swearing, or, rather, promise that they won't do that again. The motives why he did it didn't matter at that point once they said that was not something they inattended to do, nor will they do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I will try to take us back to your statement. On page 12, you say that when you arrived at the Vrgin Most police station they presented a list of accusations against that person and those were that she entered Krajina without valid documents, that she was a foreigner, that she took UNPROFOR troops to certain areas without approval of local authorities, that she spread misinformation. My question to you is this: Were any of the accusations against that person, the accusations that you heard about at the Vrgin Most police station, was any of it correct and true?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said to you earlier, she was an interpreter whose job was to go along with either the police, the UN civil police or the military, wherever they wanted to go. She didn't voluntarily -- I replace, she didn't determine where that was. And any case, we had freedom of movement for every -- of that area, so the accusations I rejected them all as meddling and uncalled for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, could you please look at the following page in your statement, which is page 13, paragraph 1. Here you speak in some detail about Lazarevic. And you say, amongst other things, that Lazarevic was the kind of person who could be a good mercenary. You say that he was a person whose ideals and life goals changed quite often. Why did you describe Slobodan Lazarevic in these terms?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, the person I was trying to remember was Toso Paic. I just remembered the name. Toso Paic was at that time the person who was responsible for police and that is the third person I mentioned in my earlier statement. Yes, on the latest question about Lazarevic, it was a long series of interaction with him where he changed roles, attitudes, attire, everything, and by that I mean on the first week of my arrival he was not even with the local authorities. He presented himself as an interpreter for EC monitors. EC at that time, the predecessor to EU. Then for awhile he changed again and presented himself as an interpreter to Toso Paic or to Cedo Bulat. Then he -- there was a lot of changes of roles, attitudes, and everything. By the time we concluded the mission, he was wearing the same uniform as the local troops, local Serbian forces, carrying a gun, and basically being one of the troops. So there was a lot of reasons that led to that conclusion, all of them being summarised as seeing one person metamorphasise from one role to another, from a civil to a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, he also appeared on radio and he broadcast sundry speeches which fueled up the rhetorics amongst the Serbs in Sector North; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was broadcast in the local language, and the only reason I came to know about them was because they were received in Karlovac by the Croatians who were angered by the broadcast which he made from the top of Petrova Gora. And I did go and talk to him and he took the light in issuing those sundry broadcast. He didn't even deny them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the second paragraph on the same page. Was Lazarevic also mixed up in the attempts to corrupt or compromise the sector commander, the commander of Sector North, that is? Could you please look at the second paragraph from the same page.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could somebody highlight it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in on the second paragraph of the same page on the right-hand side, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I regrettably had to come to that conclusion that comes as the attempt to compromise the sector commander, yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in 1999 Lazarevic was charged with defrauding a number of persons of considerable amounts of money? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, counsel. That particular aspect of his activities didn't reach me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In view of your impressions of him, are you surprised to hear that he was charged with a crime of multiple frauds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection as to relevance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Withdraw the question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: During your tour of duty in the former Yugoslavia from 1991 to 1995, did you ever see or meet a person whose name is Franko Simatovic and who is also known as Frenki?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my recollection, but again this -- how many years since 1992? If it is not in my testimony that I had met him, then I don't recall, but Simatovic is a name that rings a bell, but I don't know in what connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I reviewed your statements and there is no reference to Mr. Simatovic in any of them, but let's move on. Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I'm looking at the clock, you now took after the break 25 minutes. How much -- and again, I'm sorry to that I have to establish that where I specifically asked you to assist the Judges by referring to the pages of those -- of what is in evidence, that, for example, this example of the interpreter which was arrested, what she was charged with, whether the witness believed this, it's all found on page 15389 of the Milosevic testimony. The witness has answered all those questions which you are putting to him now again, apparently satisfied with the same answers as he gave at the time, and just referring us to a statement which is not in evidence. So you are doing exactly all those things I invited you not to do and if you would not have done that, you might have finished your -- concluded your cross-examination in 20 minutes. You have three minutes left, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, between April 1992 through March 1994, did you ever go to the headquarters of the 21st Corps at Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the date but I recall making an extensive tour of Petrova Gora with both Cedo Bulat and maybe, I don't recall who else was there. I was impressed by that place. The date is not particularly memorable to me, but the visit I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, in this period between April 1992 and March 1994, did you in the area of Sector North see any Special Police forces, Special Police, that is from the Republic of Serbia in that area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't know the -- or distinguish is more correct, if the Special Police that I saw almost daily around the sector were across the border from what would be then Bosnia-Herzegovina or they were indigenous. They were moving freely between that border. And there was no signs in terms of uniform or markings that would enable one to make a distinction other than they were Serbian in affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say Serbian units, and this is throughout all of your statements, you are referring to units of the local Serb population, in other words, units from the then Republic of Serbian Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was trying to explain. Some were in the so-called Serbian Republic of Krajina which we simply knew as Sector North of the UNPA, and those who were across the border in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were north Serbian Republic of Krajina, but Srpska Republika, I can't remember the exact name they use for when they were across, but there was nothing to distinguish them by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic, the headquarters you were talking about, the headquarters of -- the headquarters of the 21st Corps at Petrova Gora, were you referring to the headquarters of Mr. Bulat?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I read from you what is in evidence: "Q. Did Colonel Bulat also have a headquarters in Petrova Gora? "A. Yes, that's a wooded forest behind there. "Q. And did you visit what -- that command centre? "A. Yes. "Q. Can you briefly describe what the centre is like?" What is the purpose of asking this witness whether he went to these headquarters where it is clearly in evidence that he has been there? What is the purpose of asking the same questions and apparently you were not concerned about the answers -- yes, but I really have difficulties in understanding why you apparently have ignored page 15404 and asked the witness the same questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was not my intention. My expectation was that the witness will give a different answer to that question. In other words, I had reason to believe that he went there on several occasions and had he confirmed that, then I would have followed that up with other questions. However, he answered the way he did and I did -- I have to say that I did have my reasons to ask him whether he had gone there on a number of occasions and his answer what it was, but I do have to try and bring some context to what I want to ask about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you then have to do, Mr. Petrovic, in order to also make clear to the Chamber what you are doing, then you say to the witness, You testified in the Milosevic case that you visited the Petrova Gora headquarters. Did you go there more than once? Question takes approximately 15 seconds, you know exactly what you want to know. If he went there more than once, you can continue, and then we, as judges, we know in what context you put that the question, that's one, namely related to the Milosevic testimony. I specifically invited you to assist us by referring to what we find and what is in evidence instead of going to areas -- to documents which are not in evidence, that's one. Second, it would have been immediately clear to us what the purpose of your question was. So try to remain focused on these matters because it's really -- it's really disturbing our focus. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have been able to verify the authenticity of 2D99, that's the Karadzic/Abdic declaration of 22 October 1993, so if it is tendered from the bar table, the Prosecution will not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way the agreement is also covered by the Milosevic testimony, so therefore it would have assisted us as well to be taken there instead of to be taken to statements which are not in evidence. Mr. Jordash are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, Mr. Jordash would like to further cross-examine you on a certain matter. Mr. Jordash, you indicated this is on the basis of new material, I take it whenever you touch upon such material that you tell us to what extent it's new since the 26th of August, 2009, because that, of course, justifies your re-cross examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I was also hoping to elaborate on the overall issue of the UN hostages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you justified your request by referring to new material. Whenever you touch upon such material, please indicate that that was new for you and when you received it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, so that there's no difficulties, I would, with Your Honours' leave, like to go a little bit wider than the new material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't stop you from doing that, but I was just exploring what that new material was and if you want to go a bit further, then we'll see how much time you need for that and see whether you could have done it at the earlier occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should indicate at this stage that some of the new material are new instructions as well as some new documents. I should say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then next time if you ask for permission to do so, then please be precise in your wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kirudja. The sole issue I'd like to ask you questions about is the UN hostages with an aim to clarifying what happened and with an aim to clarifying the role of Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask that we turn to your statement, 2D325, page 56 of the English and page 57 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I want to start, Mr. Kirudja, if I may, with questions to clarify your knowledge concerning Milosevic's relationship with the Bosnian Serb authorities. Now, looking at the third paragraph down the page, you make the point that: "Although rarely overt, I believe Belgrade's influence in the RSK was considerable. Milosevic could engineer the ouster and ascendancy of RSK officials and their policies, but was subtle in his control." Then the next paragraph down, you make the point that: "Milosevic's control over RSK or RS officials seemed to vary with time, depending on events in the region." And a bit further in that same of paragraph, you make the point: "A few years later," with reference to the Vance Plan, "however, Babic was again on Milosevic's good side when Martic joined in common cause with Karadzic, and both Martic and Karadzic fell out of favour with Milosevic." Now, with reference to these points and with reference to early 1995, are you able to assist in explaining briefly what the cause -- or, sorry, what the relationship was between Milosevic and Karadzic as you saw it just immediately prior to the hostage crisis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, Your Honour, as much as I knew in the reports I prepared. There was very little of substance or significance that I didn't include in the report that this is a paragraph summarising that. I couldn't add much more to the background of that report, and certainly not 15 years later in recollection. What I want counsel to bear in mind is that as the paragraph says, there's a time-line to that relationship. This was picking specifically to the difficulties inherent in the taking and release of the hostages, specifically where I came in at the request of your client that I communicate some assistance that was needed through -- from the UN commander at that time to help them release these remaining hostages without further harm because they felt that it was not going to be easy for them because of that strained relationship, so that was the point of all of that. It's not an analysis of the relationship between the two people. It's the context in which it was being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you make the point in the same paragraph that there were statements -- this is the last three lines of the second to the bottom paragraph: That there were statements -- sorry, that: "Milosevic's brief comments also indicated that Milosevic retained the loyalty of Mladic even when he, (i.e., Milosevic) closed the FRY/BiH border." Now, first of all with reference to the closure of the border, what time-period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I don't remember dates as much as events as the time has passed. So would you be specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. Say in May of 1995 before the hostages were taken, was there a closure of the border, and in your view how effective was it at that point?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall the border was closed as part of differences between those who were -- those who were on the Bosnian side in control on the Serb side and Milosevic, so he did close that border, and he did invite observers from EU, so that the observations as to how effective the closure of that border was I couldn't speak to because that responsibility was transferred and placed in the the hands of EU monitors. At that time the head of that monitors was a person I knew well and consulted very often with, a colonel from Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And through that -- sorry, did I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, you didn't. I was struggling to remember the colonel's name from Sweden who commanded that observer unit. I did discuss with him many times, he would update me. From what I was discussing with him, there was relative success in controlling the border, I emphasise, from discussing with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And trying to understand your remark there from Mladic, were you aware of Mladic's reaction to the border being closed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from Mladic point of view. The reference to Mladic here is what I gleaned from Milosevic himself talking about Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware from Milosevic how often immediately prior to the UN hostage crisis how often he was in contact with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know. He normally wouldn't talk in that kind of detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware of the relationship between Mladic and Karadzic at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me take you to May of 1995 precisely. Were you aware of increasing military operations by Muslim and Bosnian Serb forces around Sarajevo at that point as the backdrop to the taking of the UN hostages?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe somewhere in my testimony I did mention that as a background, but not to a great detail, but we were aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Wasn't the Muslim forces attacking and pushing the Serbian forces towards the river Drina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about that great detail. The only part I'm emphasising was in context of this exercise of taking hostages. We did have to examine all the risks including that kind of activity to our objective being, of course, to secure the release of the -- all the hostages unharmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware that the UN commander General Rupert Smith had requested the Bosnian Serb army to surrender mortars before the 25th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only spoke to him directly on the matters of the hostages, I mean General Rupert Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware of attacks by the American and Spanish planes on the VRS around the 25th of May, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- at a place called the Ravna mountain?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware that Akashi had demanded that the Muslims and the Serbs withdraw their heavy weapons from around Sarajevo on the 26th of May?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean, our head of operations --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Akashi? No, only in general, I only remember him when he asked Milosevic and others to help have everybody comply with the requirement of UNPROFOR, but not to that specificity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Do you recall -- I'm looking at the 26th of May, the NATO attack on Serb positions near Pale?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the one preceding the taking of hostages?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware it was of a great discussion after the hostages were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. And what was the nature of that attack and how quick was the hostage taking after that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, we just knew one day they had all been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At that point am I correct that 145 UN military observers were taken in the first instance?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, I'm not right now completely in touch of the details how many were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware of the overall political context with France, for example, demanding that the peacekeepers be protected by the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The overall, yes, I would. In fact, the reaction I'm describing was all nations where the hostages were at risk or taken were all, of course, interested in the outcome of that exercise, and by interested, meaning released and released unharmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Pentagon had ordered aircraft carrier and other armoury into the Adriatic Sea in response to the hostage taking?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At what point were you approached to become involved?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an initial release, again I forget the time and date and the number, and then there was reluctance to release the balance of the hostages. At that time Akashi and others we met in Belgrade and as is represented -- representative in Belgrade was tasked after that to liaising with the authorities in Belgrade to have the hostages released and in the course of that, I did meet with Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll come to that shortly. I just want to see if there's some of the background you might be able to confirm. I appreciate your answers so far and I understand if you can't. Were you aware on the 27th of May of the seisure of more hostages, bringing the total to around 200?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware there were minimal left and unreleased than there were initially released. At the point I was talking to your client, some had been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Were you aware that on the 27th of May, Bosnian Serb military personnel disguised as French peacekeepers captured 12 free French peacekeepers in central Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, is there any risk that one of your previous question may have been misunderstood? You asked: "Were you aware on the 27th of May of the seisure of more hostages, bringing the total to around 200?" Which means 55 more than you earlier mentioned. The answer was: "I was aware that there were minimal," minimal is maybe a mistake, "that there were left unreleased -- that there were more left unreleased than there were initially released." But apparently your question was about increasing the number of hostages rather than not releasing all of them. The answer is apparently about not all of them being released only a smaller number, so others remaining. Whereas your question, apparently was about increasing the number of those who were taken hostage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer and the question seem not to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I'll ask the question again, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Kirudja, was the following: Were you aware that Serbs, Bosnian Serbs, had seised more hostages on the 27th of May, bringing the total to over 2 -- to around 200?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of that particular date, I don't recall exact knowledge that they had added to the hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of -- or did you -- were you told about the information service of the General Staff of the VRS issuing a statement in response to taking -- in response to their taking of hostages, a statement which effectively said that in response to NATO attacks, the hostages have been taken and will remain detained?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That specific statement I couldn't say I am aware. What I was aware of was there were hard-line statements being made of not wanting to release the hostages and that some harm would befall those which had not been released if NATO didn't desist from the position they had held, that member of the air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And those hard-line statements included reference to UNPROFOR now being considered to be --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- part of the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of those hard-line statements, was, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were you aware at the time that they were emanating from Mladic and those close to him?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware where the hard-line positions were coming from, other than an earlier statement you referred to this -- the relationship between Milosevic on the one side, Karadzic and the others on the other side having deteriorated to the point of closing the border, policy shift. And I have testified to this on a great length about what it was, the split was. They wanted to go one way, the other group wanted to go another way, policy-wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. On that subject, during your time within the former Yugoslavia, had you observed the relationship between the Bosnian Serb authorities and the Serbian authorities as worse than it was at the time of the hostage crisis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took the fact that it went to the extent of Belgrade authorities closing the border as that relationship having significantly turned a corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Was it known at the time that President Chirac, at around the 27th of May, had telephoned Slobodan Milosevic and appealed to him to use his influence to have the UN hostages released?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware who it is he might have been acting because he was influenced. What I am aware of is that it was very clear to him and a lot was at stake that those hostages be released unharmed and quickly. And he, I mean Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware that the president of Russia, Boris Yeltsin had sent a special envoy, Aleksandr Zotov, to visit Slobodan Milosevic to make the same request for him to use any influence to release the UN hostages?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not particularly that envoy. It was also common knowledge when I was in Belgrade it was a stream, a long, long, stream of representatives from the groups that were interested, and specifically the contact, the six that included Russia, Germany, and others. That was a specific group that was quite active in seeing events in the broader context of Yugoslavia resolve in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear about the attack on the 27th of May, 1995 where UN soldiers tried to surrender their positions to the Muslim forces in the area of Vrbanja bridge?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware by the end of May that several UN personnel had been killed as a result of clashes between Bosnian Serb and UN and also Muslim forces and UN?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word is UN personnel. The personnel there was a range of soldiers, police, civilian, what personnel are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: UN peacekeepers.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Peacekeepers, all of them were all peacekeepers whether soldiers, civilians --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, soldiers. I beg your pardon, sorry.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I ask that question because of course we had some deaths by some other unexplained circumstances in different places, but I couldn't be sure which one you are entirely talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there, from your perspective, a very real fear that these hostages would be killed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh yes. This one was unmistakable concern, both of your -- Mr. Stanisic when I met him on the few occasions, there was an unmistakable fear that those hostages would be harmed, killed, and more than that, the Milosevic side, of which your client was acting, would be blamed for it. That was abundantly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll return to that in a moment. Was there, from your perspective, also the same unmistakable fear that the way in which this hostage crisis played out might well have larger consequences for the on-going peace negotiations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Rupert himself made it clear that he wanted them unconditionally released and he commanded the forces in Bosnia and he reported to Akashi who had the last request for further NATO strikes. So there was tension all over, including further action by NATO, if anything happened to those hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was there a fear that the way in which the hostage crisis played out might well determine whether the warring parties continued to fight leading to greater loss of life?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I please have 1D1490 on the e-court. This is a new document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which you received when?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which we received on the 5th of October from the National Council. 5th of October this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to try to have you clarify, Mr. Kirudja, how these hostages were being held. If you look at the document quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think, could it be under seal, for the moment, Your Honour, I think we need to clarify it with the National Council, the status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Document not to be broadcasted, and if tendered, to be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I don't suggest that this is a comprehensive list of what was happening or which detainees were detained where, but this document perhaps gives a flavour, does it not, Mr. Kirudja, of the chaos that the hostage crisis brought to the region?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document before, so I really wouldn't know much about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you confirm this, though, that the number of hostages by the end of May in 1995 was around 470 men scattered in strategic locations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I wouldn't be the authority for those numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's put aside the numbers then. But the hostages were, by the end of May, scattered around strategic locations by the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that I can confirm that was the gist of the discussion, some known and some not known where they were at the beginning of the attempt to rescue them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This document here detailing UNPROFOR detainees, does that accord with your general impression of the type of scattering of these hostages in different towns and villages and at strategic locations such as bridges and so on?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing is what is in my testimony, and Mr. Stanisic made clear they were in different locations and different places, some which he knew, others he didn't. Actually, never supplied me any of these locations when I was talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we go to page 2 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that these -- the nationalities mentioned are familiar with you -- familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The nationalities are familiar in the sense that I had knowledge of what nationalities comprised the various forces that are deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this as an exhibit under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1490 becomes Exhibit D141 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I also, just very briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted as such under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sorry. May I play a video at this point. It's been played to you when you gave evidence in direct, but I'd like just to show you a very brief section. P50, 33 minutes and 12 seconds to 33:46 seconds. And although there's a voice-over, we aren't playing the video for the purposes of the voice-over, just for the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not one of the two which was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What we've just seen there, was that your understanding of how the hostages, the several hundred hostages were being held, handcuffed and detained against posts and bridges and ammunition dumps and the like?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I could generalise from what I saw, even if, in fact, one of those I met in person and is a Canadian soldier. I don't think I can generalise to everybody who was being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough. But some of the several hundred were being held such as that, and you were aware of that when you began your involvement in the issue; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were aware they were being held. How, where, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You must have become aware, though, during the process that some were being held out in the elements, handcuffed to bridges and the like?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular video, I repeat, is familiar. I even know that soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's a surprise to me.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Canadian.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
