utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Would you agree that by the end of May the stakes were getting higher, if I can put it like that, the French had sent an aircraft carrier and it was moored alongside Croatia, for example?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware then from -- just more generally, that there was talk from the international community about an intervention force, a military intervention to rescue the hostages?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know what they were doing, where we were trying to get them released.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You didn't hear any of this? Wasn't this the context in which you were involved?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. Okay. Fair enough. Let me take you then to Mr. Stanisic. Did you meet him for the first time around the 9th of June?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, the dates are particularly -- the dates themselves, that I met him, yes. On that particular date, I met him more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me are try to assist, and we'll have some of your notes up on the screen so we can work from this reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have P48.17 on the screen. It may be under seal. I'll just check very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, my records indicate that it's not under seal. It's a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can check that, could you tell us what the document is, how it's described?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's -- I'm looking for the 9th of June notes relating to Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that code cable to Mr. Akashi?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's 48 -- P4817, I think. Should be. And it's a -- yes, Your Honour, it's a code cable from Mr. Kirudja to Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal with events just shortly before this, if you are able to deal with those events relating to Mr. Stanisic, but just to orientate yourself, was this the first time you had met Mr. Stanisic or had you met him prior to the 9th of June?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I can't say that the dates are particularly awful to me. I know that I met him more than once and I don't know whether this is the first time or the last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your evidence clearly was that you met him only in relation to the hostage crisis --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not at any other moment. That's the evidence you've given until now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that assist you, or would you like to see whether the 8 of June or the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The 9th of June, as I understand it from Mr. Kirudja's previous evidence, is the third phase of the release of the hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I right, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the last phase?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I was saying I don't know whether that's the last time I met him or the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's what I was trying to clarify, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with the contents and maybe that will help to see if you had met him before. On the 9th of June, you meet Mr. Stanisic and you describe him as the special envoy to President Milosevic. And Mr. Stanisic is anxious about recent developments on the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 or where?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Mr. Stanisic was concerned about what particularly? Was that a reference to the shelling by the UN personnel that we see described in paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I alluded to it earlier in my comment today, that we were apprehensive of the conditions when these hostages were still being held and there was fighting such as being described in paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Now, was Mr. Stanisic concerned about the condition that the hostages found themselves in?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, he made clear he had the task of securing their release unharmed. He was worried that not only the hostages still were in danger, but he, himself, would also be at considerable risk going there as he planned to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what impression did he give you about that danger to himself, from whom?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the forces opposed to Milosevic's policies that were holding the hostages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I think this was asked before for the witness. Apart from that, of course, this is certainly not a new document, this apparently then is within the framework of the new instructions, but certainly this document doesn't justify the further cross-examination. But if you then also ask questions which the witness explained already, because that's already part of his evidence, what he was -- how he understood what Mr. Stanisic had said to him. Please proceed, but keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I have on the screen please, 1D1484, please. This, I think, is a new document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't stop you on the previous one, I just said, it's not new. If you want to further cross-examine him, please don't put the same questions that were already asked to the witness, but apparently you decided to move on with the next document which you said is a new one which you received also.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I thought I would -- I'm going to return to that subject but I thought I'd do it in the context of the new documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the new documents you received October this year as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We found it on the EDS collection and we found it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's -- was it on the EDS collection on the 26th of August, 2009?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've perhaps spoken too quickly. I imagine it was but I can't confirm it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you have no date after the 26th of August which you firmly can tell us that you only then received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's how I understood you, We found it after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is a document -- have you had a chance to read it, Mr. Kirudja, please?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware of this document signed by Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm the underlying events that around this time 120 people were -- 120 UNPROFOR detainees were released?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note, Your Honours, dated 2nd of June; right? It's dated 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just flashed a document where I'm talking about your client and it's dated 9th of June, the previous document. I have testified that by the time I went to see Mr. Stanisic, some hostages had been released. The only thing I can say this may be part or some of those already released. Not more than that or no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you briefed before meeting Mr. Stanisic concerning the role that Mr. Stanisic was then playing in terms of the hostages and their intended release or hoped-for release?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only role I knew is that he was trying to secure their release.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you told about his meeting on the 27th or 28th of May with Karadzic and Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you told about his meeting with Mladic at around the same time, about two days or the day -- a day later?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you told anything about the demands that the Bosnian Serb authorities, and I include both civilian and military, were making in relation to the release of the hostages?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the context when we met in Belgrade about it with Mr. Akashi, Milosevic. The demands, in general, were discussed and they are on record, and it was about the unfairness of NATO attack, and thus context I am aware and this might form part of my testimony in the meeting with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware that before Mr. Stanisic became involved, there had been talks between General Rupert Smith, French General Bertrand de Lapresle and Mladic concerning the hostages which had been unsuccessful in persuading Mladic to release them?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, the meeting I am referring to where I'm aware of the general discussion, those meetings where Akashi will come there, General de Lapresle but not Rupert Smith, so, in that context, what was made available for knowledge to me was that general context of what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware in a general way that there had been approaches to Mladic outside of the Stanisic role which had been unsuccessful?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically. Again, I only know he had been cautious about it and considered it a very risky operation for the reasons I have already testified about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have please on the screen 1D1504. This is a new document which we -- which we found but I'm not sure exactly when. But it's an article by Misha Glenny.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you aware of this writer, journalist?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to page 2, and the section I'm interested in is halfway down the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just for your information, this is an article by Misha Glenny into organised crime and he writes, halfway down the page or a third of the way down the page: "It was not until I researched a single instant from the Yugoslav war ten years ago that it dawned on me what was going on. Nationalism, ethnic hatred and religious fanaticism were mere blinds serving to obscure the real cause of these wars, money and human greed. At the end of May 1995, the Bosnian Serb leaders Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic seised several thousand peacekeepers in retaliation for the UN mandated bombing of Serb positions around Sarajevo." Then just to save time, moving further down: "Milosevic sent his chief of security Jovica Stanisic to sort out the mess. Stanisic had witnessed more than his fair share of dirt during the war, and if anyone could cajole the Bosnian Serbs into releasing the hostages, Stanisic was your man. But not even he was prepared for what greeted him when he reached their headquarters. Karadzic and his deputy were taking receipts of bags of cash from the government of Greece, 20 million in used notes, funded unknowingly by Greek taxpayers in exchange for the hostages."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would start reading further, "Stanisic blew a gasket."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "Stanisic blew a gasket telling Greek ministers more or less to bugger off and warning the Bosnian Serb leadership of dire retribution from Belgrade if the deal went ahead. He succeeded (and was later thanked and congratulated by the British and American intelligence services for his troubles)."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Does any of this description trigger off anything that you know or heard?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, mildly. I mean, in the sense that it's a different opinion from others' opinions that one has heard about the reasons why things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'm looking at the clock, I don't know how much time you would need more, you are close to the one hour you asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think another 10 minutes should do it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm also looking at Mr. Stanisic, what would be best to do. Mr. Groome, would you -- would there be any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the moment I just have one question for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I then suggest since the Chamber, as matters stand now, have no questions for the witness, that you take your ten minutes, then we'll hear the one question, then I don't know whether you would have any additional questions at this moment in response to the

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we -- you have consulted with Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I will consult if I can now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can the witness ask for a five-minute break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness can ask for a break. Mr. Jordash, whatever the outcome is, we'll have a five-minute break anyhow, but then the question is whether it should remain a five-minutes break or whether we make it immediately half an hour break because if we take a five-minute's break that is not sufficient for changing the tapes, which would cause us to have a break anyhow at later stage which I would like to -- let me just check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking for technical aspects of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber decided. We'll take the long break now otherwise things become too complicated. We'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, 10 minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I've just got a few remaining questions, Mr. Kirudja, perhaps I will be testing your memory again and I apologise. Are you able to confirm that approximately 120 UNPROFOR soldiers were released across the border post at Karakaj, the border of Bosnia and Serbia on the 3rd of June?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there were released. Exactly that border, no, I'm not -- I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. But you are aware of this release. If I said to you that this contingent consisted of French, British, Swedish, Danish, and Ukrainian and Canadian, would that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about this? I take it it's all well documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd have to refresh my memory before I agree, would I agree to any reasonable facts put forward that are supported by public knowledge of these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, have you tried to seek agreement on the matter? At least I hardly can imagine that you stay divided forever on this data.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we are not divided --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. I just -- I just wanted to make clear that we should elicit evidence from witnesses where -- on matters which are reasonably in dispute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall the question?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and my answer is that I honestly wasn't keeping tabs of how many or what nationality, but I was aware, again I repeat, there was a bunch of released hostages before I started engaging Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me deal with it then quite generally. Were you aware of releases through the beginning of June, the 3rd and the 6th and the 12th of June and thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of a period of time when they were being released on [indiscernible] was how they were being released, the last of which culminated to the last batch being released and we have talked about it. There is a video about it here played in this courtroom about the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And can we just have on the e-court, please, 1D1485, a new document we found on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's a 13th of June, 1995, order by Karadzic. And if you just have a look at that, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've taken note of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Does that accord with your recollection of the events, in particular the hands-on approach taken by Mr. Stanisic in being present at the hand-overs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that particular aspect only. There are other details that are -- I'm not privy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this as an exhibit, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just saw this document, just notified of it today that it's going to be used. We are in the middle of trying to check the provenance of the document, of course I will agree to it if I can verify its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be MFI'd. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document 1D1485 becomes D1421 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. D1421 keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we have 1D01491, please. A new document, a Security Council resolution adopted by the Security Council on the 16th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you have a quick glimpse at the front page, please, Mr. Kirudja. Are you familiar with this Security Council resolution?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you go to the operative paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I missed what you said.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we go to the operative paragraphs of the resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2 then. The particular paragraph I wanted to refer you to was the paragraph beginning about a third of the way down the page where it says: "Underlying once again the urgent need for acceptance by the Bosnian Serb party of the Contact Group peace plan as a starting point opening the way to the negotiation of such an overall peaceful settlement." And am I correct that around this time of this resolution, there were on-going difficulties and hostages remained detained?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you are taking that paragraph to mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not, I'm asking you the overall context before I ask you about that paragraph. The overall context which gave rise to the Security Council resolution?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to speak to that. Normally anything headed to the Security Council has a very, very, broad context that I wouldn't be testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Second question then: Would you agree with this, that the hostage crisis was -- or occurred within the context of a desperate determination on the international community to bring the Bosnian Serbs back to the negotiating table and back to the -- back to a commitment to the Contact Group peace plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would defer with your characterisation of it. The Security Council was not desperate. It was driving the events that were happening there at this point. It was -- the Security Council resolutions that were operating and operating in the entire area, this being one of the many series of resolutions the Council had passed. So I wouldn't characterise it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, you would agree that the -- there was a consensus amongst the international community that the way forward was through the Contact Group peace plan and that required the Bosnian Serbs to recommit to it? You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't testify to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think, as a matter of fact, if you would know that these are very composite questions, the the last one was, Mr. Jordash. This one is. Is there anything you could say about what apparently was raised by Mr. Jordash as to consensus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a sense at that time that something positive was happening in the sense that I recall this was one of the first time or pretty much the unprecedented action of striking at Serbian targets by NATO precipitating their action of hostage taking, then releasing them, and there was a sense that things -- a little more firmness did produce results and the Council was reflecting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, how long do I have left, if anything, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could ask, but I think it would be one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I have on the screen please, 1D1487 received from the National Council on the 5th of October, 2010, under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: While that is being -- 1D1487.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did I say 1D8487? I meant 1D1487.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: While that is being found, Mr. Witness, can I ask you this: Were you aware that Mr. Stanisic had taken a proposal by Chirac to the Bosnian Serbs during this crisis to persuade them to return and join the Contact Group negotiations for peace?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of his detailed activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this is a slightly different subject, but were you aware of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, when I said one minute, I really meant it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I was I waiting for a document to come on the screen for 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just ask one question. Were you aware, Mr. Kirudja, that upon the return of the hostages, soon thereafter within days, the Bosnian Serbs returned to the negotiating table to discuss the Contact Group peace plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just alluded in my earlier answer that a little more firmness did produce results and that was being appreciated, that the international community through the Security Council, through NATO was a lot more determinate at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was a very practical, whether upon return of the hostages, whether within days, the Bosnian Serbs returned to the negotiating table, could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't confirm that it was within days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you can confirm that they did return to the negotiation table after relatively short period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No further questions. But may I tender the document on the screen from the bar table, if nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the document on the screen would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D1487 becomes Exhibit D143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. No need to have it under seal. Mr. Groome, you had one question. Do you still have one question? Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, Mr. Jordash has spent considerable time establishing the difficult, dangerous, and tense situation that was the UN hostage crisis. My question is simply: Does the fact that Mr. Stanisic was able to go into Bosnia and extract the hostages without the use of force or without any loss of life, in your view, indicate something about the authority and influence he had during that period?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a conclusion, I certainly did draw that he was influential against all those odds that he had already indicated he was going to meet, yet he succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kirudja, I have one -- let me first see, do you have any questions, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question. An article written by Misha Glenny, at least a portion of it, was read to you. It said that at the end of May 1995, the Bosnian Serb leaders, Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic seised several thousand peacekeepers in retaliation for the UN mandated bombing of the Serb positions around Sarajevo. The several thousand peacekeepers that were seised, is that comes -- does that come close to your perception at the time of the number of peacekeepers that were seised?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly I don't think though in thousands. I think there were less than 1.000. If I'm wrong, because the numbers that I saw in buses last time, the last batch released, were not in thousands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. There appear to be no further questions for you, Mr. Kirudja. I'd like to thank you very much for -- not only for coming, but for coming back after more than one year to conclude your testimony. I think last time the 26th of August, I said I don't know where you are going but please arrive safely there. I would like to thank you for having answered the questions of parties and of the Bench, and I wish you the same as I did last year, wherever you go, arrive safely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. You are very kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could Mr. Kirudja be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: While that's being done, may I apply to tender two documents which I referred to but didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could do that. I'm not stopping you, but I'm looking at the clock and I know what is still on our programme today which might be of greater urgency than to deal with this relatively --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll leave it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of course important matter, but nothing is lost if we deal with that after a couple of days. Could we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We will adjourn for the day and we'll resume on Wednesday, the 17th of November, quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom, and I publicly apologise for the late conclusion of this session. I hope that there's some understanding for the reasons that caused it to happen. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of November, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 22 23 24 25
